near_miss.lead: Guards at a stronghold ask an arriving man who he is.
near_miss.why_not: Close narrative situation, but the asking and arrival verbs are not cognate; fortification vocabulary plus a copula cannot establish an inherited inquiry formula.

near_miss.lead: Coming home / going to the house.
near_miss.why_not: Norse kemr and Sanskrit jagmur continue the come/go root, and garðr and gṛha are potentially comparable house/enclosure vocabulary. But garð occurs with Norse gengr, not kemr; ordinary homeward movement, with neither distinctive wording nor a shared figure.

near_miss.lead: Father and mother as a pair.
near_miss.why_not: Both parent words are cognate, but the passages express different relations: a gift from father to mother, actual parents present or raising a child, and Vedic cosmological parents. The natural kinship pair alone does not distinguish inheritance from independent phrasing.

near_miss.lead: Same night / people born in one night.
near_miss.why_not: The Norse same-word modifies evening or men; the Homeric expression says that two men were born on one night. Shared roots are not a shared collocation.

near_miss.lead: Falling or lying at a ruler’s feet/knees.
near_miss.why_not: Norse supplication is coherent and repeated, but the retrieved Greek foot expressions mean men encountered in the way or infantry, not supplication; the Vedic ox passage concerns walking and ploughing. No two-branch slab witness to the proposed gesture formula.

near_miss.lead: Red apple in an interpersonal or erotic setting.
near_miss.why_not: Norse æpli rautt and Serbian rumenu jabuku have cognate apple and red material; Serbian corpus searches confirm further red-apple uses. Yet apple redness is a natural attribute. The Norse apple conceals a letter, the Serbian witnesses mark lovers or compare a child’s complexion, and the Irish red adjective describes the rath, not its golden apples. Late romance and collected song do not supply a distinctive inherited construction.

near_miss.lead: Lying/staying through the night.
near_miss.why_not: Norse ligia ... nott and Old Russian noščь ... ležaščju share lie and night roots but merely state overnight lodging. Greek has a different residence verb. No marked formula or congruent ritual/poetic function.

near_miss.lead: Hanging on a tree or wooden support.
near_miss.why_not: Search for tree plus hang returned the Norse threat, two further Germanic occurrences (one false tree hit involving a trough), and the Hittite ritual. Hittite hangs ritual objects; Norse threatens to execute men on the highest tree. Cognate action and material do not provide the same distinctive context or syntactic construction.

near_miss.lead: Bearing gold.
near_miss.why_not: Norse requests carrying as much gold as possible; the Russian imperative concerns taking golden keys. Gold is an object in one and a modifier in the other; the surrounding retainer vocabulary does not repair the mismatch.

near_miss.lead: Sister and wife.
near_miss.why_not: The Norse marriage proposal identifies the addressee’s sister as the speaker’s prospective wife. The birchbark letter negates two relationships in a dispute. Cognate kinship nouns, but different predicates and pragmatic structures.

near_miss.lead: Coming at midnight; middle of the night.
near_miss.why_not: Exact Norse/Latin come + middle + night correspondence, supplemented by Greek middle-night phrases within the slab. Searches found varied ordinary uses, including drinking, waking, medical timekeeping and travel; some root-pair hits had middle modifying day or summer instead. This is a temporal expression freely attached to arrival, with no distinctive inherited poetic function. Not promoted to a claim.

near_miss.lead: Nights and days as continuous duration.
near_miss.why_not: Norse day/night merism and the Old Russian prayer-duration expression agree semantically, but day vocabulary is renewed and the pair is a universally available time merism. Other Greek witnesses contrast successive night and day events, not continuous totality. The Christian chronicle does not independently secure inheritance.

near_miss.lead: Sleep and rest.
near_miss.why_not: Norse hvíla and sofa occur in two separate instructions about a wedding bed and household sleeping; Latin somnus ... quiete describes insomnia with sleep covering the eyes. Cognate roots but no equivalent predication or distinctive phrase.

near_miss.lead: Leaving/lending a sword.
near_miss.why_not: Norse liá takes the sword as loaned object; Latin relinquere concerns Orestes leaving a sword behind. Even allowing historical root association, the acts and literary settings differ and the sword words are not cognate.

near_miss.lead: Greatly love / greatly benefit.
near_miss.why_not: Norse unna ... mikit describes affection; Greek mega ... oninēsi describes benefit, while Hesiod has a noun phrase great benefit. An intensifier beside historically related predicates is insufficient to demonstrate an inherited phrase across this semantic and syntactic gap.

near_miss.lead: Choosing or being acceptable among suitors.
near_miss.why_not: Norse velia and kaus occur in a woman’s reproach over her chosen husband. Vedic juṣṭā vareṣu wishes the girl acceptance among suitors. Choice/pleasure roots co-occur in a marriage setting, but the participant roles, syntax and speech acts differ; this does not establish a fixed inherited marriage formula.

near_miss.lead: A ruler’s yoke removed from the neck.
near_miss.why_not: The slab partners concern grafting and exposed bones, not political servitude. Wider corpus search found Greek yoke-of-subjection parallels, recorded separately as a search lead. There is no second cross-branch slab anchor to this metaphor.

near_miss.lead: Drink induces sleep; carrying a sleeper to bed.
near_miss.why_not: The Irish deug suain is an administered sleep draught, whereas Norse describes intoxication followed by sleep and carrying the woman to bed. The bear root in Irish belongs to giving battle elsewhere in the sentence. Sanskrit describes a tired army sleeping. Common sleep vocabulary and motif do not establish shared wording.

near_miss.lead: Eating apples.
near_miss.why_not: The Latvian cows eat marsh grass and are later released into clover; ābolā has been read as apple by the mapper. It is not an object of eating and is not an apple here. The apparent Norse/Latvian phrase is false.

near_miss.lead: Dark night / darkness of night.
near_miss.why_not: Norse myrct af nott states darkness caused by night before fighting ends. Serbian addresses night as full of darkness or speaks of its darkness in a parallel lament. The night and darkness roots correspond, but syntax and poetic function do not; corpus search returned the same two Serbian anchors only. An obvious natural association is insufficient.

search_lead.cognate: Norse ok (dative oci) and Greek ζυγόν continue *yugóm, yoke; neck and removal predicates are lexically different.
search_lead.argument: The Norse ruler’s death lifts his yoke from the speaker’s neck and ends tribute. Theognis refuses to put his neck beneath an enemy’s yoke; Persae describes release from a yoke of power. These are congruent political uses beyond literal animal harnessing, unlike the slab partners. A useful inherited-metaphor candidate for review, but late Norse romance and the Christian yoke idiom found in the same corpus leave diffusion or independent metaphor possible; no claim of demonstrated inheritance.
